Discussions on distribution and dispensing LH in Section 4.3.1.3 are applicable to LNG due to 2 its cryogenic nature. LNG refueling flow rates are limited not by pump power alone but by thermodynamic constraints preventing flash vaporization and managing differential temperatures between aircraft tanks and hoses. Current cryogenic transfer operations suggest flow rates of 100–600 L/min (43-258 kg/min) (Chart Industries 2014), substantially lower than Jet A hydrant systems that routinely exceed 3,000–4,000 L/min (Refuel International n.d.). To give an estimate of fueling times, a Class 8 LNG truck with single tank of 120 gallons requires close to 3 minutes to fuel (DOE 2019). LNG leaks differ fundamentally from Jet A spills. Jet A forms pools that burn; LNG rapidly vaporizes into a cold methane cloud. A spill typically vaporizes within minutes, depending on wind and surface heat. The principal hazards include: 81 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 1. Flammable vapor cloud formation, which can ignite if it reaches an ignition source. 2. Asphyxiation or cold-burn danger for personnel in proximity. 3. Rapid phase transition when LNG contacts water, causing explosive vaporization. Emergency procedures must prioritize immediate area evacuation, vapor cloud tracking, ventilation, controlled ignition, and isolation of cryogenic transfer systems. Compared with Jet A, LNG introduces new detection requirements and new training for ramp personnel. Firefighting agents and methods must be revised as well. If LNG leaks or is jettisoned, it will evaporate nearly instantaneously upon exposure to ambient conditions at altitude, creating a plume of methane that disperses rather quickly but can have adverse effects for the environment. Methane-fueled aircraft would, therefore, plan to use engine burn-off rather than fuel jettison. This operational difference may lead to modified emergency procedures. Atmospheric impacts of methane releases would likely trigger new ICAO guidelines for controlled venting and environmental reporting. 4.3.3 Ethane LE is stored at cryogenic temperatures of −89°C at atmospheric pressure; it is less volatile than liquid hydrogen and more volatile than LNG.
